subject: Art & Design
source: National Curriculum (Art and Design). Drive Art & Design folder reviewed (Elements of Art deck, KS3 files) and the school's 'Art - Y9' lesson plan example used for format and the Y9 Zentangle topic.

lessons.title: Colour theory: the colour wheel and mood
objectives: Explain warm and cool colours and complementary pairs
Use colour to create a mood

keywords.def: red, yellow and blue: colours that cannot be made by mixing
colours made by mixing two primaries: orange, green, purple
colours like red, orange and yellow that feel hot
colours opposite each other on the wheel, such as blue and orange

starter: Bismillah. Name the three primary colours.

teach.heading: The colour wheel
bullets: Colours sit in a circle in order
teach.note: Pupils need colouring pencils or paint, paper, a pencil. Show a colour wheel on screen. Pupils draw a circle and divide into six.

teach.heading: Mixing secondaries
teach.note: If using pencils, layer lightly. Misconception: mixing always makes brown; this happens with too many colours.

teach.heading: Warm and cool
teach.note: Ask pupils to sort items: sun, ice, forest, fire. Show how complementary pairs create contrast.

teach.heading: Colour and mood
teach.note: Link to calm and wellbeing; mention Allah's creation of sunsets. Do not use faces.

teach.heading: Planning a mood picture
teach.note: Abstract shapes: circles, waves, triangles. Pupils choose a mood word.

practice: Mix red and blue. What colour?
independent: Complete a six-colour wheel and label primary and secondary colours.
Sort six objects into warm and cool lists.
exit: Create an abstract picture using only warm colours; then one using only cool colours.
Write a sentence about the mood of each.
homework: What mood do cool colours give?
lessons.send: Find three warm and three cool colours in your home and list them.

lessons.title: Symmetry and design: a four-fold tile
objectives: Draw a design that is symmetrical in four sections
Use a plant shape as inspiration

keywords.def: when one side is a mirror image of the other
the line you can fold along to make two matching halves
a single design that can be repeated
a flowing design based on plants and curves

starter: Name a warm colour and a cool colour.

teach.heading: Symmetry in nature
bullets: A snowflake has many lines of symmetry
teach.note: Show a leaf. Ask for lines of symmetry. Pupils need paper, pencil, ruler, colouring pencils.

teach.heading: Arabesque designs
bullets: Used on walls, books and tiles
teach.note: Show photos of arabesque tilework. Explain that artists used curves, leaves and flowers.

teach.heading: Four equal sections
bullets: Draw a square 10 cm by 10 cm
Draw lines to split it in four
Draw a motif in one section
teach.note: Model on a board. Ask what happens if we flip the motif to each section.

teach.heading: Reflecting the design
bullets: Copy the motif as a mirror image
Do it for all four sections
The corners meet in the middle
teach.note: Common error: copying without flipping. Show with a mirror or tracing paper.

teach.heading: Colour and finish
bullets: Repeat the same colour in matching places
teach.note: Remind them of the colour wheel. Matching colours keep the symmetry.

practice: Draw one line of symmetry on a leaf.
How many lines of symmetry has a square?
independent: Draw a motif in one quarter of a square and mirror it into the next.
Check with a mirror or fold.
exit: Complete a four-fold design based on a plant shape.
Colour it using a complementary pair.
lessons.send: Design a second tile with a different motif and compare.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Environmental artists and assistive technology (Tomorrow's World)
lessons.title: What is land art? Andy Goldsworthy and patterns in nature
lessons.bigQuestion: Can art that will blow away tomorrow still be worth making?
objectives: To understand what land art is and how artists use natural materials and patterns
successCriteria: Some: explain why land art is often temporary
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: noticing signs of Allah in nature

keywords.def: art made in nature from natural materials
something from nature, like leaves or stone
lasting a short time
a repeated design

hook.text: Can art that will blow away tomorrow still be worth making?
hook.a: Yes: it teaches looking, it can be photographed, and it reminds us nothing in this world lasts.

islamicLink.text: After describing rain, crops, palms, olives and pomegranates, Allah says: 'Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe' (Al-An'am 6:99). Nature is full of signs.

starter.q: Name one thing you budgeted for in Spring 1 PSHE.

teach.heading: Land art
bullets: Made outdoors from what is found
teach.note: Andy Goldsworthy (British, born 1956) arranges leaves, stones and ice; show images of his works only where no people appear.

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.why: It changes or disappears; photos record it.

practice.q: Name the pattern in a fern leaf.
practice.a: A spiral as it uncurls and a branching pattern in the leaves.
practice.model: I do: a pine cone shows spirals; a leaf shows branching veins.

independent.q: Sketchbook (or pupil PDF): sketch three natural objects from home or garden and label each pattern.
independent.model: The teacher sketches a leaf's veins on camera.

independent.q: Extend: write why temporary art can still matter.
independent.a: It trains looking and gratitude; photos keep it.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Can art that will blow away tomorrow still be worth making?
exit.a: Yes: it teaches looking, it can be photographed, and it reminds us nothing in this world lasts.

lessons.homework: Collect five natural or recycled items (with an adult) for next lesson.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Environmental artists and assistive technology (Tomorrow's World)
lessons.title: Planning a land-art piece: composition and balance
lessons.bigQuestion: What message about the earth would you like your art to share?
objectives: To understand how to plan a land-art composition with balance and a clear message
successCriteria: All: sketch a plan for my piece
Some: choose a message and explain how the design shows it
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and science: environment and recycling

keywords.def: how parts are arranged
parts look evenly weighted
strong differences, such as light and dark
an idea the art shares

hook.text: What message about the earth would you like your art to share?
hook.a: For example: care for creation, change of seasons, or nothing is wasted.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And it is He who has made you successors upon the earth' (Al-An'am 6:165). As caretakers, we can use art to remind people to look after the earth.

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: Light petals on dark soil create ...

practice.q: Sketch a radial plan using leaves and stones.
practice.a: A circle plan with items radiating from the centre.
practice.model: I do: a stone in the middle, rings of leaves, then a ring of twigs.

independent.q: Pupil PDF: plan your land-art piece: message, materials, sketch and where you will photograph it.
independent.a: A full plan with message and sketch.
independent.model: The teacher plans 'seasons' with green to brown leaves.

independent.q: Extend: write how your design shows your message.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: What message about the earth would you like your art to share?
exit.a: For example: care for creation, change of seasons, or nothing is wasted.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Environmental artists and assistive technology (Tomorrow's World)
lessons.title: Making and photographing land art
lessons.bigQuestion: A photo can make a small arrangement look big. How?
objectives: To understand how to make my land-art piece and photograph it well
successCriteria: All: arrange my materials following my plan
Most: photograph it from a good angle in good light
Some: reflect on how the message comes across

keywords.def: place things carefully
the direction a photo is taken from
brightness that shows detail
think about what you made

hook.text: A photo can make a small arrangement look big. How?
hook.a: Getting low, filling the frame, and choosing a plain background.

starter.a: For example: care for the earth.

starter.q: Best light for photos is often ...

teach.heading: Make it
teach.note: Short week: keep making to 40 minutes.

teach.heading: No people in photos
teach.note: House rule.

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

check.q: To show a whole circular pattern, photograph it ...
check.why: From above shows the whole pattern.

practice.q: Watch the teacher photograph an arrangement. Which angle worked best?
practice.a: Directly above, with the arrangement filling the frame.
practice.model: I do: I try side, low and above; above shows the pattern best.

independent.q: Make your land art (finish at home), photograph it from two angles, upload the best photo with a one-sentence message.
independent.a: A finished piece, two photos and a message.
independent.model: The teacher arranges and photographs a small piece on camera.

independent.q: Extend: write which photo is better and why.

exit.q: Photos of our art should show ...
Back to our ponder: A photo can make a small arrangement look big. How?
exit.a: Getting low, filling the frame, and choosing a plain background.

lessons.homework: Finish and upload your land-art photos.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Environmental artists and assistive technology (Tomorrow's World)
lessons.title: DT: assistive technology and user needs
lessons.bigQuestion: Who in your family might find an everyday task hard, and what simple tool could help?
objectives: To understand what assistive technology is and how designers start from a user's needs
successCriteria: All: name three everyday assistive tools
Most: describe a user's need clearly
Some: write a design brief for a product
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: forces and grip; Computing: accessibility features

keywords.def: tools that help people do everyday tasks
the person a product is for
something the user must be able to do
a short statement of what to design and for whom

hook.text: Who in your family might find an everyday task hard, and what simple tool could help?
hook.a: For example, a grandparent with stiff hands: a jar opener or a thick pencil grip.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever relieves a believer of a hardship of this world, Allah will relieve him of a hardship of the Day of Resurrection' (reported by Muslim). Designing to help others is a good deed.

starter.a: the person a product is for
options: the person a product is for

teach.heading: Everyday assistive tools
teach.note: Objects only.

model.problem: Write a brief for a pencil grip
steps: User: a Year 2 child who finds pencils hard to hold
Product: a card or foam grip
Criteria: fits a pencil, soft, stays on
model.answer: Design a soft grip that fits a standard pencil and helps a young child hold it comfortably

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

options: what to design and for whom
check.why: A brief names the product, user and needs.

practice.q: Write a user need for a page holder.
practice.a: 'The user needs pages to stay open without holding them.'
practice.model: I do: user: someone reading while writing notes; need: hands free while the book stays open.

independent.q: Pupil PDF: choose a user (no names of real people) and write a design brief with three criteria for a pencil grip or page holder.
independent.a: A brief with user, need, product and three criteria.
independent.model: The teacher writes the brief for a page holder.

independent.q: Extend: list two materials you could use and why.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Who in your family might find an everyday task hard, and what simple tool could help?
exit.a: For example, a grandparent with stiff hands: a jar opener or a thick pencil grip.

lessons.homework: Ask a family member about one task they find hard; note it for your brief.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Environmental artists and assistive technology (Tomorrow's World)
lessons.title: DT: designing and making a prototype
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do designers make cheap prototypes before the real product?
objectives: To understand how to design, make and test a card prototype that meets my brief
successCriteria: All: make a template and cut it out
Some: test it with the user's need in mind and improve it
lessons.smsc: Moral: perseverance and learning from mistakes

keywords.def: a first model to test an idea
a shape to draw round
check it works
improve step by step

hook.text: Why do designers make cheap prototypes before the real product?
hook.a: To test ideas quickly and fix problems before spending time and money.

teach.heading: Joins and shaping
teach.note: Scissors with adult supervision.

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

options: To get the size right before cutting card
check.why: Templates save materials and improve accuracy.

practice.q: Watch the teacher make a rolled-card grip. How many layers?
practice.model: I do: roll a card strip three times around the pencil, tape inside, slide off and test.

independent.q: Make your prototype (finish at home), test it against your three criteria and make one improvement; photograph and upload.
independent.a: A prototype, a test table and one improvement.
independent.model: The teacher tests the grip on camera.

independent.q: Extend: record what you changed and why.
independent.a: For example: added foam for comfort.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Why do designers make cheap prototypes before the real product?
exit.a: To test ideas quickly and fix problems before spending time and money.

lessons.homework: Finish testing and bring your prototype to the next lesson.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Environmental artists and assistive technology (Tomorrow's World)
lessons.title: Evaluate: brief, prototype and land art
lessons.bigQuestion: If a real person used your prototype every day, what would they say?
objectives: To understand how to evaluate my prototype against the brief and reflect on my land art
successCriteria: All: say which criteria my prototype met
Some: suggest a final improvement for a real user
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest evaluation and kind feedback

keywords.def: judge how well it worked
facts from testing
the finished version
comments to help improve

hook.text: If a real person used your prototype every day, what would they say?
hook.a: Answers vary: what works, what is uncomfortable, what could be better.

teach.heading: Gallery
bullets: Star and wish in the chat

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share the results and explain the right answer and why the others are wrong.

options: 'It fitted the pencil and stayed on; foam would make it more comfortable'

practice.q: Write one evaluation sentence with evidence.
practice.a: 'My page holder kept the book open for 10 minutes, meeting criterion 1.'
practice.model: I do: criterion, test, result: 'It stayed on when shaken: criterion 3 met.'

independent.q: Pupil PDF: evaluate the prototype (criteria table and paragraph) and reflect on your land art; give a star and a wish to two classmates.
independent.a: A full evaluation and two peer comments.
independent.model: The teacher evaluates a sample prototype.

independent.q: Extend: how could your product be made in a factory?
independent.a: A moulded plastic or foam version.

exit.q: Back to our ponder: If a real person used your prototype every day, what would they say?
exit.a: Answers vary: what works, what is uncomfortable, what could be better.

lessons.homework: Show your prototype to the user you designed for and note their feedback.
